DTECH-CTX-G2.title: Lanternfish design notes and retrospective
DTECH-CTX-G2.text:
LANTERNFISH - DESIGN NOTES AND RETROSPECTIVE
Author: Dashiell Marrow, SRE I, Cindervale Systems. Written December 2025 for the SRE team wiki.

Problem
The checkout path (cart-api -> pricing -> payments-gateway) had a p99 of about 1,380 ms against an SLO target of 900 ms. Traces showed unexplained gaps before outbound calls that no span covered. We suspected DNS but had no per-pod data. CoreDNS exposes metrics per CoreDNS replica, only for the queries that reach it, and it sees a client's search-domain expansion as several unrelated queries rather than one slow lookup.

Design
Lanternfish is a Rust sidecar built on the tokio async runtime, using the hickory-proto crate to parse DNS messages. It is injected into pods on the checkout path.
- The pod uses dnsPolicy None with a dnsConfig whose first nameserver is 127.0.0.1. Lanternfish listens on 127.0.0.1:53 over UDP; only the sidecar container gets the NET_BIND_SERVICE capability.
- Each query is forwarded unchanged to the cluster DNS service IP. Lanternfish times the lookup from the moment the query arrives from the application to the moment the response is written back.
- It exports a Prometheus histogram, lanternfish_lookup_seconds, with 12 buckets from 1 ms to 2.5 s and the labels qtype, rcode and upstream. The queried name is deliberately NOT a label, to keep cardinality bounded.
- A counter, lanternfish_search_expansions_total, counts queries for names that end in one of the pod's search suffixes and come back NXDOMAIN.
- The existing Prometheus scrapes it every 15 seconds; no new storage was needed.
- The second nameserver line in dnsConfig points straight at the cluster DNS IP, with options timeout:1, so a crashed sidecar costs a one-second retry rather than an outage.

Why a sidecar
We considered three options:
1. CoreDNS metrics. Already existed, but aggregated per replica rather than per pod, and blind to how many expansions one application lookup triggered.
2. An eBPF probe on each node. Per-pod data without touching pods, but our GKE nodes ran Container-Optimized OS, nobody on the team had written eBPF before, and we estimated 4 to 6 weeks.
3. A sidecar. Per pod by construction, easy to remove, and about 2 weeks of work.
We chose the sidecar. The trade-off: it only sees pods it is injected into, and it adds one local hop to every lookup.

Rollout
Lanternfish ran on the 14 deployments of the checkout path for three weeks.

Findings
- 31% of p99 latency on the checkout path came from DNS resolution.
- The main cause was the default ndots:5. External names such as the payment processor's API have fewer than five dots, so the resolver tried every search domain first. On GKE that meant up to 10 failed queries (A and AAAA for each of 5 search domains) before the real lookup.
- A smaller share came from occasional 5-second stalls caused by a known conntrack race when A and AAAA queries go out in parallel over UDP.

Fix
- Priya Oduya (senior SRE) reviewed the design and ran the rollout of the fix; I wrote the sidecar, the dashboards and the analysis.
- Checkout-path pods moved to ndots:2, and the three external payment endpoints were changed to fully qualified names with a trailing dot.
- NodeLocal DNSCache was enabled on the cluster, which also removed the conntrack stalls.
- Checkout p99 fell from 1,380 ms to 910 ms, and DNS dropped to about 6% of p99.

Overhead and limitations
- Median added latency is about 0.3 ms per lookup; each sidecar uses about 6 MiB of memory and under 5 millicores of CPU.
- UDP only: queries that fall back to TCP after a truncated response are passed through and not measured.
- After the fix we removed the sidecar from 9 of the 14 deployments and kept it on 5 as a canary.
- It was never deployed to the other two clusters, and it has not been open-sourced.

DTECH-CTX-G1.title: Quarrystone take-home: Pager Quiet Windows (problem statement)
DTECH-CTX-G1.text:
QUARRYSTONE ANALYTICS - PLATFORM TEAM TAKE-HOME (v3)
Problem: Pager Quiet Windows

Background
Our on-call tool lets engineers schedule "quiet windows" during which non-critical pages for a host are held back. Engineers create windows independently, so the list for one host arrives unsorted and often overlapping. Before we push windows to the pager we collapse them into the smallest equivalent list.

Part 1: merge_windows(windows, grace)
Input:
- windows: a list of pairs [start, end], in integer minutes since the start of the quarter. A window covers minute start (inclusive) up to end (exclusive), so [10, 20] covers 10 minutes.
- grace: an integer number of minutes.

Rules:
1. If any window has end < start, raise ValueError with the message "inverted window at index i", where i is the index of the FIRST such window in the input list as given (before any sorting).
2. A window with end == start covers no time and is dropped silently. A dropped window must not bridge two other windows.
3. After sorting by start, a window merges into the current merged window when its start <= current end + grace. Windows that touch (next start == current end) therefore always merge, even with grace 0.
4. Grace only decides whether two windows merge; it never extends a window. A merged window ends at the largest end among the windows it absorbed.
5. Return the merged windows sorted by start, as a new list of [start, end] pairs. Do not mutate the input list or the pairs inside it.

Examples
Example 1: windows = [[10, 20], [15, 30], [40, 50]], grace = 0
Output: [[10, 30], [40, 50]]

Example 2: windows = [[5, 10], [10, 12], [13, 20]], grace = 0
Output: [[5, 12], [13, 20]]
([5, 10] and [10, 12] touch, so they merge. The gap from 12 to 13 is 1 minute, which is larger than grace 0.)

Example 3: windows = [[5, 10], [10, 12], [13, 20]], grace = 1
Output: [[5, 20]]
(Note the result is [5, 20], not [5, 21]: grace never extends a window.)

Example 4: windows = [[30, 30], [1, 4], [2, 3]], grace = 5
Output: [[1, 4]]
([30, 30] is dropped; [2, 3] lies inside [1, 4].)

Example 5: windows = [[0, 10], [11, 11], [12, 20]], grace = 1
Output: [[0, 10], [12, 20]]
([11, 11] is dropped before merging, so it cannot bridge the gap between 10 and 12.)

Example 6: windows = [[7, 3], [1, 2], [9, 4]], grace = 0
Raises ValueError("inverted window at index 0")

Example 7: windows = [], grace = 10
Output: []

Part 2: total_quiet_minutes(windows, grace)
Return the total number of minutes covered by the output of merge_windows. A gap that grace bridged is counted, because the merged window spans it. For Example 1 the answer is 30, for Example 3 it is 15, and for Example 7 it is 0.

Constraints
- 0 <= len(windows) <= 200,000
- 0 <= start, end <= 10^9
- 0 <= grace <= 60
- Your solution must run in O(n log n) time. Our reference solution runs in under 1 second in Python for n = 200,000.
- Python 3.10+ or Go 1.22+. Standard library only.

What we look at
Correctness on our hidden cases (including every edge case above), readability, the tests you write yourself, and a short note (under 200 words) explaining your approach and its complexity. Please do not spend more than 3 hours.

Live follow-up
In the follow-up interview we will ask how your design changes if windows arrive one at a time from a stream and the pager needs to ask "is minute t quiet?" at any moment.

DTECH-CTX-C1.title: Quarrystone take-home candidate FAQ
DTECH-CTX-C1.text:
QUARRYSTONE TAKE-HOME - CANDIDATE FAQ
Forwarded by Pilar Okonkwo-Reyes, Technical Recruiter. Compiled from questions earlier candidates asked about the Pager Quiet Windows exercise. Different interviewers wrote different answers.

Q: How long should I spend on it?
A: Please keep it under 3 hours. We are not grading polish.

Q: How big are the inputs?
A: Each host has at most 200,000 windows, so an O(n log n) sort-based solution is what we expect.

Q: Do windows that touch, like [5, 10] and [10, 12], merge when grace is 0?
A: No. Ends are exclusive, so [5, 10] and [10, 12] stay separate unless grace is at least 1.

Q: What languages can I use?
A: Python 3.10+ or Go 1.22+, standard library only.

Q: Can I use sortedcontainers or another package for part 2?
A: Yes, any package on PyPI is fine as long as you pin it in requirements.txt.

Q: What does the grader check first?
A: The edge cases. Touching windows always merge, even with grace 0, and zero-length windows are dropped. Most failed submissions get one of those wrong.

Q: What is the performance bar?
A: The hidden cases go up to 2 million windows per host, and the reference solution finishes in under 1 second in Python. If yours takes a few seconds that is fine; we cut off at 5 seconds.

Q: When is it due?
A: You have 48 hours from when the link opens. Most people spend a full day on it.

Q: Should part 2 count grace gaps as quiet time?
A: No, only minutes actually inside a window count.

items.question: Before we start, have you ever built a double-entry ledger? Either way, design one for grower payouts: the tables, how a payout moves money between accounts, and how you guarantee a retried payout never pays twice.
items.answer:
I haven't built a production double-entry ledger, but I've worked on idempotent, event-driven payment flows, so let me design one.

Tables: accounts (id, owner_type, currency), journal_entries (id, idempotency_key unique, created_at), and postings (entry_id, account_id, amount, signed). Every entry's postings sum to zero.

A payout: debit the grower-payable account, credit the grower's cash account, in one transaction. Escrow holds sit in a separate liability account until settlement releases them.

For no double pay: the idempotency key on the entry is unique, so a retry hits the constraint and returns the original entry instead of posting again. The bank transfer itself carries the same key, so the provider dedupes too.

USER (spoken): Can the array have duplicates?
INTERVIEWER: Yes, but the output shouldn't repeat a triplet.
USER (spoken): Okay, I'll sort it, then for each index run two pointers on the rest and skip duplicates as I go.

items.question: walk me through abba
conversation:
NATIVELY: The bug is that `enumerate` gives you `(index, char)` tuples, so `ch` is a tuple and `right` is never defined. You want the index as the loop variable and the character as the key.

```python
def length_of_longest_substring(s):
    seen = {}
    left = 0
    best = 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        if ch in seen and seen[ch] >= left:
            left = seen[ch] + 1
        seen[ch] = right
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best
```

The `seen[ch] >= left` guard matters: without it, a character seen before `left` would wrongly pull the window back.
items.answer:
ABBA is a classic synchronization problem, usually framed as two threads sharing a bounded buffer: a producer that adds items and a consumer that removes them. The tricky part is that you can't just lock the whole buffer, because then the producer and consumer can't work at the same time, so you use two counting semaphores, one tracking empty slots and one tracking filled slots, plus a mutex to protect the buffer itself.

The producer waits on `empty`, locks the mutex, inserts, unlocks, then signals `full`. The consumer does the mirror image: waits on `full`, locks, removes, unlocks, signals `empty`. The semaphores handle the blocking and the mutex handles the mutual exclusion, and the order matters, you acquire the semaphore before the mutex, otherwise you can deadlock.

If you meant the ABBA deadlock pattern instead, that's the case where two threads each grab two locks in opposite order, thread one takes A then B, thread two takes B then A, and they wedge. The fix is a global lock ordering so everyone acquires in the same sequence.

items.question: Let's warm up. Two sum: given 2, 7, 11, 15 and a target of 9, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to it. Approach and complexity, please.
items.answer:
The classic approach is a hash map: walk the array once, and for each number check whether its complement, target minus the current value, is already in the map. If it is, return those two indices. Otherwise store the current value with its index and keep going. For 2, 7, 11, 15 with target 9, at index 0 the complement is 7, not seen yet, so store 2. At index 1 the complement is 2, which is in the map, so return **0 and 1**.

Time is **O(n)** since it's a single pass with O(1) map lookups, and space is O(n) for the map in the worst case.

items.question: What's the time complexity of this: the outer loop runs i from one to n, and inside it j starts at i and doubles each time while j is less than n, doing constant work per step.
conversation: INTERVIEWER: Sorry I'm a couple of minutes late, my last meeting ran over.
INTERVIEWER: Did you get caught in the rain coming in? It's been pouring here all morning.
USER (spoken): A little, but the train was on time, so I can't complain.

items.answer: The outer loop runs n times, and for each i the inner loop doubles j from i up to n, so it does about log(n/i) steps. Summing that over i gives **O(n log n)**. The doubling is what makes the inner loop logarithmic rather than linear.

items.question: heapify complexity?
items.answer: Building a heap from an array is **O(n)**, not O(n log n). The intuition is that most nodes sit near the bottom and sift down only a level or two, so the work sums to a constant times n. Each individual sift-down is O(log n), and popping the min or max n times is O(n log n).

items.answer:
The bug is that `enumerate` gives you `(index, char)` tuples, so `ch` is a tuple and `right` is never defined. You want the index as the loop variable and the character as the key.

```python
def length_of_longest_substring(s):
    seen = {}
    left = 0
    best = 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        if ch in seen and seen[ch] >= left:
            left = seen[ch] + 1
        seen[ch] = right
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best
```

The `seen[ch] >= left` guard matters: without it, a character seen before `left` would wrongly pull the window back.

items.question: Don't write code yet. Count the islands in a grid of ones and zeros, except the grid is huge, millions of rows, and you can only stream it one row at a time with memory for about two rows. How would you approach it?
items.answer:
The key constraint is that you can't hold the whole grid, so you track connectivity incrementally as rows arrive. Keep a label array for the current row, where each cell gets a component id, and a union-find over those labels to merge components that touch. When a new row comes in, you compare each cell to the one above it and to its left neighbor: if both are land, you union their labels; if only one is, you inherit that label; if neither, you start a new component. Once a row is fully processed and you've moved past it, any component that no longer appears in the current row can never connect to anything below, so you finalize it and increment your island count. That way memory stays proportional to one row's worth of labels plus the union-find, which is what keeps it within your two-row budget.

The subtlety is that a component can stay "open" across many rows, so you only close it when it drops out of the active row. That's what makes the count correct rather than overcounting each time a shape reappears.

items.question: Write a function that returns true if a string is a palindrome once you ignore case and anything that isn't a letter or a digit. So 'A man, a plan, a canal: Panama' should be true and 'race a car' should be false. Talk me through it as you go.
items.answer:
Here's the two-pointer version. I normalize on the fly instead of building a cleaned copy, so it's O(1) extra space.

```python
def is_palindrome(s: str) -> bool:
    left, right = 0, len(s) - 1
    while left < right:
        while left < right and not s[left].isalnum():
            left += 1
        while left < right and not s[right].isalnum():
            right -= 1
        if s[left].lower() != s[right].lower():
            return False
        left += 1
        right -= 1
    return True
```

Two pointers start at the ends and walk inward. Each inner loop skips characters that aren't letters or digits, then I compare the two survivors case-insensitively. If they ever differ it's false, and if the pointers meet or cross, everything matched.

Time is O(n) since each character is visited at most once, and space is O(1).

items.question: So if you joined and owned this, what would you change first, how would you know it worked, and what would you leave alone?
conversation: INTERVIEWER: So some context on our side. Right now we page on any service whose 5xx rate is over 1 percent for five minutes.
USER (spoken): Same threshold across every service?
INTERVIEWER: Same threshold everywhere. On-call gets roughly 90 pages a week and people have started muting the channel.
INTERVIEWER: About half of those fire during deploys and clear on their own.
items.answer:
The first thing I'd change is the threshold itself. One percent over five minutes is the same for a service that gets ten requests a day and one that gets millions, so I'd move to SLO-based, multi-window burn-rate alerts per service, and add a deploy-aware suppression window so the half that fire during deploys and clear on their own stop paging anyone.

I'd know it worked by watching pages per week drop and the muting stop, and by tracking how many pages actually needed a human.

What I'd leave alone is the paging path itself, the routing and escalation, since that's not the problem here.

items.question: Let's start simple. What's the difference between a process and a thread?
items.answer: A process is an independent program with its own address space, so processes are isolated from each other. A thread is a unit of execution inside a process, and threads in the same process share that memory and resources. That makes threads cheaper to create and switch between, but a crash or race in one thread can take down the whole process.

items.question: We have an endpoint that lists shipment events newest first, and new events are being inserted constantly while people page through it. How would you design the pagination so nobody sees duplicates or skips anything?
items.answer:
Offset pagination breaks here because new inserts shift the window, so you get duplicates and skips. I'd use **keyset pagination**: order by a stable, unique key, typically a monotonic event id or a composite of created_at plus id as a tiebreaker, and page with a cursor that says "give me the next N rows where that key is less than the last one I saw." Since the sort key is unique and immutable, each page continues exactly where the previous one ended, so inserts at the head don't disturb the pages behind them.

The cursor is opaque to the client, just the last key encoded, and I'd return it alongside the results. One caveat: if events can be backfilled with an older timestamp, a reader could miss them, so I'd either make the key strictly monotonic or accept that and document it. For the newest-first case, the first page has no cursor and later pages pass the last id.
